lesson.title: Making Gametes: An Overview of Meiosis
lesson.summary: Meiosis is a specialized division that takes one diploid cell through two successive divisions to produce four genetically unique haploid gametes.
lesson.body:
Producing gametes, sperm and eggs in animals, requires a kind of cell division that ordinary mitosis cannot provide. Mitosis takes one diploid cell and produces two diploid daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell, which is exactly right for growth, tissue repair, and asexual reproduction, but exactly wrong for making gametes. As covered in the previous chapter, a gamete needs to be haploid, carrying only one set of chromosomes, so that fertilization can safely restore the diploid number without chromosome counts doubling every generation. Meiosis is the specialized division that accomplishes this.

Meiosis begins, like mitosis, with a diploid cell that has already completed a normal S phase, so every chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids. From there, though, meiosis diverges sharply from mitosis: instead of one division, it involves two successive divisions, called meiosis I and meiosis II, with no additional round of DNA replication in between. The result is not two diploid daughter cells but four haploid daughter cells, each genetically distinct from the original cell and from each other.

The two divisions are not redundant, each does a different job. Meiosis I, covered in detail in the next chapter, separates the two members of each homologous chromosome pair from each other, which is the step that actually reduces the chromosome number from diploid to haploid. Because of this, meiosis I is sometimes called a reductional division, and it has no real counterpart in mitosis. Meiosis II, by contrast, separates sister chromatids from each other, using essentially the same mechanics as an ordinary mitotic division, just carried out in a cell that is already haploid.

Meiosis is also the reason sexual reproduction generates genetic variation. Two features unique to meiosis I, the pairing and crossing over of homologous chromosomes and the independent assortment of which homolog ends up in which daughter cell, are covered in the coming chapters, and both ensure that the four haploid cells produced by meiosis carry new combinations of alleles never present together in either parent chromosome. That variation, generated fresh in every round of gamete production, is a large part of why offspring resemble but never exactly duplicate their parents.
